In brief

Two paragraphs after someone in Burke's pub asks "Who's astanding this here do?" the question is posed again more insistently because the drinks have been passed around but the bartender has not yet been paid. It was Stephen who took the orders and now it is Stephen who is urged, none too gently, to cough up. The speech here takes a turn away from Scottish idiom to Cockney-like speech. A number of the words come from current London dialect, as does the pronunciation when someone notes that Stephen has "near free poun" in his pockets.

At more length

The bartender, evidently looking expectant, becomes an authority to be placated—"Waiting, guvnor?"—and one or more voices rush to register the justice of his inquisitive glance and assure him that payment is imminent: "Most deciduously. Bet your boots on. Stunned like, seeing as how no shiners is acoming." "Deciduously" seems to be a silly play on "decidedly" or "definitely," and "Bet your boots" is a common way of saying "You bet"—i.e., "certainly." If the barman seems stunned it is because no "shiners" have yet crossed his counter. This ancient English word (the OED traces it back to the 14th century) began to be applied to bright gold and silver coins in the late 18th century. By the late 19th it was used as a term for money in general.

More twisting of the English language ensues as someone asks, "Underconstumble?" Gifford observes that Eric Partridge documents "understumble" as a common play on "understand" and he plausibly surmises that Joyce here maps that neologism onto "underconstable." If he is right, the word may be taken as mocking the English habit of bowing to authority. Now the "guvnor" is a constable on his beat, and he is asked, Understand, officer?

Attention turns to Stephen: "He've got the chink ad lib. Seed near free poun on un a spell ago a said war hisn." "Chink" is another ancient English word for coins, inspired by the sounds they make knocking against each other in a purse or pocket. Brewer's Dictionary notes that "It was formerly in good repute as a synonym for coin," and Gifford calls it "Cockney slang." Slote, Mamigonian, and Turner, citing Eric Patridge, gloss "ad lib" as an abbreviation of ad libitum, "as much as one likes." They note that both expressions are documented in Heinrich Baumann's Londinismen (1902), a German study of London slang and cant that Joyce consulted. So too is "hisn," employed as someone says (here translated) that he "saw nearly three pounds on him a while ago that he said was his"—referring to the moment earlier in Oxen when Stephen fills his companions' cups and says, "See ye here. And he showed them glistering coins of the tribute and goldsmith notes the worth of two pound nineteen shilling that he had, he said, for a song which he writ. They all admired to see the foresaid riches in such dearth of money as was herebefore."

Slote and his colleagues judge that these two sentences are delivered "in a strong Scottish accent," as in the previous paragraph, but the London idioms would argue for a more English inflection. This hunch is confirmed by someone's pronunciation of the word "three" as "free." In southeast London and some other working-class English regions, the voiceless "th" sound becomes "f": I fink so, You owe me free pounds. (The same "th-fronting" converts voiced "th" sounds into "v": Stand furver away, I know your brover.) This "th-fronting" was documented in London as early as 1787 and became widely recognized as a feature of working-class speech in the 19th century. For someone reading these sentences aloud, a full-blown Cockney patter would probably not be amiss.

More English dialect resonates when someone reminds Stephen that coming to Burke's was his idea: "Us come right in on your invite, see? Up to you, matey. Out with the oof." The word "mate" needs no discussion, but the obscure "oof" is another distinctly English term for money. Gifford calls it "Cockney slang," and Slote, Mamigonian, and Turner observe that it comes from "the Yiddish expression ooftish, popular in London in the late nineteenth century, which derives from the German auf Tische (properly auf dem Tische), 'on the table', because one refused to play cards for money unless the cash were on the table." (The expression, they note, is documented both in Partridge's dictionary and in Baumann's Londinismen.) One of the men who beheld Stephen's wealth says, then, "You invited us here, mate. Your treat. Out with the money."

The amount is specified in Dublin slang: "Two bar and a wing," two shillings and a penny. (The Slote team notes that five bottles of Bass, three pints of Guinness, one ginger cordial, and one absinthe should cost slightly more than this—"presumably Joyce's" mistake.) But a final London expression enters when the speaker ribs Stephen over importing some bad habits from Paris: "You larn that go off of they there Frenchy bilks? Won't wash here for nuts nohow." The term "bilks" (cheaters, swindlers) is documented in Londinismen.

John Hunt 2026
